candidates.text:
Founders, don’t get pissed off if a VC that politely passes on you, then subtly trash talks you to other VCs.

A VC that politely passed on us a while ago, recently told another VC (who I was pitching) that they thought I was a grifter. Grifter is about the most offensive thing a VC can call a founder, in my mind, while still being conveniently vague. And it’s not the first time I’ve seen this pattern.

The point of this post is that I used to get offended by VCs that politely passed on us, then covertly trash talking us. But the more I’ve thought about it, the more I realized how inevitable it is.

It’s heavily in the interest of the VC that passes (especially early/single-stage VCs and junior VCs, which this one was), for everyone else to also pass, since they’ll look stupid, or worse, if that ends up being a bad decision. “Show me the incentive, and I’ll show you the outcome.” As Charlie Munger used to say. In this case the incentive is very clear, and so the outcome is somewhat unavoidable.

So why shouldn’t founders be pissed off about it? Because fortunately most VCs, especially the ones with more experience, are smart enough to understand this dynamic, and to form their own opinions regardless 🙏👌

candidates.text:
The best sales reps solve my problems:

1️⃣ They listen to my actual problems and show me the best solution using their product — and other products. They learn my business fast, and show me exactly how their product solves my problems.

2️⃣ They help me demo, pilot or try the product in whatever fashion makes me the most comfortable.

3️⃣  They are fluent in, and honest about, the competition. This saves me time in my research. No, if your competition also has tons of customers, then they are not terrible at everything. Be honest about where you are strong, where you are equal, and where you are — for now — a bit behind.

4️⃣  They are honest about product gaps and weaknesses so I know up front. This saves me a lot of time and headaches. There is nothing worse than having to discover an important product gap after you’ve bought and deployed an app. But if I know up front, I can plan around it.

5️⃣ They don’t play games with pricing and I know the price is and will be fair from the start. This saves me a lot of time.

6️⃣  They are there for you after the deal. Yes, I know you are handing me off to customer success or whomever. But sometimes, they aren’t great and I need help. The best reps make you feel like they are always there for you, after the sale. Even if secretly, they’d rather be working on their top opportunities.

7️⃣ They’ve done research on me before the first call. They know what I do, who I am, how many employees we have, what we care about and need. This isn’t that hard. But boy it really helps. And works.

What the mediocre and poor reps do:

👿 Play (endless) games with price. I don’t have time. I know this may be all you care about, but I have a lot of other needs.

😡 Fake and pressure-filled urgency to buy now. Yes, this is an art. Practice it poorly and you are adding to my headaches. I’ll buy this month if you’ve treated me well and addressed all my needs. But no games about your generic product getting so much more expensive next month. It’s not even true.

😠 Pushing me to buy the wrong / too expensive of an edition. This can blow a deal, or undermine trust. If the simpler edition is fine for now, just sell me that.
Lies about the competition. This just makes my job of discovery and learning harder.

🙉 Not understanding my budget and situation. Don’t treat an SMB like a F500 company. Understand their budget and work to it — as a partner.

🎣 Too few check-ins. I need help.

🙅‍♂️ Too many check-ins. Leave me be.

🛑 Break-up emails. Seriously? That doesn’t help me. You should be there when I’m ready. Even if that’s 6 months from now.

🤑 Playing games on renewals. Ripping me off when we start is bad enough. Ripping me off once I depend on you is even worse.

🔚 Turning off free trials with drama. Not cool. If I need more time, just give it to me. Not everything is life has to be so transactional.

candidates.text:
Zayd Syed Ali raised $3.2M for Valley, then put on an organic marketing masterclass that companies 5-10x their size can't figure out. I studied how the founder built the organic engine, doing it:

1/ The content team is made up of only the CEO.

Zayd grew by 15K followers in 14 months, which for a founder in B2B tech is no easy thing.

And this is without any content team or agency.

Just a founder with a strong POV posting consistently about the thing he's building.

2/ His best-performing posts show the product actually working.

Zayd posts side-by-sides of a normal outbound message vs. one structured by Valley. 

One went viral off a real reply: "How the hell did you automate this?"
People don't want to be told the product is good. 

They want to watch it beat the alternative in real time.

3/ He builds in public and isn't shy about it.

Zayd treats company updates as content, and people buy into watching the company grow.

Then he mixes in memes. B2B founders showing a funny side is working right now, and the engagement proves it.

4/ Every format rests on the same pillars.

Studying his content, I can see that the content is built on these pillars: 

1. Tactical value people save 
2. A clear POV on his industry
3. Building in public 
4. Product-forward content

You don't need an expensive content team if you have a founder with a clear POV, the consistency to show up, and the willingness to prove the product works in public rather than claim it does. 

You have all you need to win.

Shoutout to @ShubhAgrawal26 who's driving a lot of the growth at Valley.
